questions.q: What is the cloud provider always responsible for, regardless of service model?
options: Configuring the customer's application settings
The customer's data classification
Which employees can access customer payment data
The physical data centers, hardware, and the hypervisor layer
questions.explain: The provider always owns the physical layer — data centers, physical hardware, and the hypervisor — no matter which service model the customer buys.

questions.q: What is the customer always responsible for, regardless of service model?
options: Replacing failed hard drives in the provider's data center
The physical security of the data center
Their own data, identities, and access control
Patching the hypervisor
questions.explain: No provider can know which files are confidential or who among a customer's employees should have access, so the customer always owns their own data and identity management.

questions.q: How does the customer's share of responsibility change between IaaS and SaaS?
options: It stays exactly the same across all service models
Under IaaS the customer manages the most (OS, patches, app); under SaaS the customer manages mainly their data and users
Under IaaS the provider manages everything
Under SaaS the customer has to patch the physical hardware
questions.explain: The customer's management burden is heaviest under IaaS and lightest under SaaS, where the provider manages nearly everything technical.

questions.q: According to real-world cloud security incident patterns, what is the most common actual cause of a cloud breach?
options: A customer-side misconfiguration, like a publicly exposed storage container or an overly permissive access rule
A flaw in the hypervisor itself
An outage in a region pair
A failure in the provider's physical hardware
questions.explain: Studies of real incidents consistently find that the provider's infrastructure rarely fails — most breaches trace back to a customer-side setting, like exposed storage or weak access control.

questions.q: Why does the shared responsibility model matter in practice?
options: It clarifies who is responsible for which part of security before something goes wrong, not after
It guarantees the customer is never responsible for a breach
It only applies to on-premises data centers, not the cloud
It is only relevant to SaaS applications
questions.explain: The model exists to make the division of security duties explicit ahead of time, so an organization knows what it still has to secure itself.
